# PyWebLib reference

PyWebLib (https://play.pyweblib.org) runs real Python 3 in the web browser (Pyodide), with no install.
It is used in schools to learn Python, and adds its own libraries on top of standard Python:

- `game`: a 2D game library (sprites, keys, mouse, collisions, sound, saving, per-game leaderboards).
- `turtle`: turtle drawing, like desktop Python's turtle.
- `game3d`: simple 3D games (shapes, a camera, the same game loop).
- `net`: multiplayer, used together with `game`.

Important when writing code for PyWebLib:

- `import game` is PyWebLib's OWN library. It is NOT pygame and has a different API. Do not use pygame calls.
- Every game has the same shape: `game.window(w, h)`, make sprites, then `while game.playing():` ... `game.frame()`.
- Coordinates are pixels from the top-left of the game window; y grows DOWNWARD. Sprites are positioned by their centre.
- `game.frame()` draws one frame and waits (30 fps by default). Put it at the end of the loop.
- Code runs in the Playground at https://play.pyweblib.org. Programs can be published to the community gallery.

A minimal game:

```python
import game

game.window(480, 360)
player = game.sprite("chicken", 240, 300, size=52)

while game.playing():
    if game.pressed("left"):
        player.x = player.x - 5
    if game.pressed("right"):
        player.x = player.x + 5
    game.frame()
```

## Printing and input

Show things on the screen and ask the user for answers.

### `print(x)`

Show something on the screen.

```python
print("Hello!")
print("Score:", 10)
```

### `print(a, b, c)`

Print several things on one line, separated by spaces.

```python
print("x", "is", 5)   # x is 5
```

### `print(x, end="")`

Print without moving to a new line, so the next print carries on.

```python
print("Load", end="")
print("ing...")   # Loading...
```

### `print(x, col="red")`

Colour the text (this works in our Playground). Any CSS colour: a name, hex, rgb() or hsl().

```python
print("Danger!", col="red")
print("Ok", col="#22cc88")
```

### `input(prompt)`

Ask the user to type something. It always gives back a string (text), even if they type a number.

```python
name = input("Your name? ")
print("Hi", name)
```

## Playground extras

A few handy things that work right here in our Playground.

### `clear()`

Wipe the output panel. Print again after it to make animations that redraw each frame.

```python
import time
for i in range(3):
    clear()
    print(i)
    time.sleep(0.5)
```

### `print(x, col="red")`

Colour a line of output. Any CSS colour works: a name, hex, rgb() or hsl().

```python
print("Win!", col="#22cc88")
```

### `input() and time.sleep()`

These pause your program, so they need Chrome or Edge in the Playground (the same as the game library).

```python
name = input("Name? ")
print("Hi", name)
```

## Variables and comments

Store values to use later, and leave notes for yourself.

### `x = 5`

Make a variable: a labelled box that holds a value. The name is on the left, the value on the right.

```python
age = 12
name = "Sam"
price = 2.5
```

### `x = x + 1`

Change a variable using its own value. Here it grows by one.

```python
score = 0
score = score + 1   # now 1
```

### `a, b = 1, 2`

Set more than one variable at once.

```python
x, y = 100, 200
```

### `# comment`

A note for humans. Python ignores everything after the #.

```python
# this line does nothing
print("hi")   # a note here too
```

## Numbers and maths

Do sums, and switch between whole numbers and decimals.

### `+  -  *  /`

Add, subtract, multiply and divide. Division always gives a decimal.

```python
print(3 + 4)   # 7
print(10 / 4)  # 2.5
```

### `//`

Whole-number division: divide and throw away the remainder.

```python
print(10 // 3)  # 3
```

### `%`

The remainder (modulo). Great for "is this even?" and wrapping around.

```python
print(10 % 3)  # 1
print(8 % 2)   # 0, so 8 is even
```

### `**`

To the power of.

```python
print(2 ** 3)  # 8
```

### `int(x)`

Turn text or a decimal into a whole number. Needed after input() for maths.

```python
n = int(input("Age? "))
print(int(3.9))   # 3
```

### `float(x)`

Turn text into a decimal number.

```python
price = float("2.50")
```

### `round(x, n)`

Round to n decimal places (or the nearest whole number if you leave n out).

```python
print(round(3.14159, 2))  # 3.14
```

### `abs(x)`

The size of a number, ignoring the minus sign.

```python
print(abs(-7))  # 7
```

## Strings (text)

Text is a string. Here is how to build it, search it and change it.

### `"hello"`

A string is text in quotes. Single or double quotes both work.

```python
greeting = 'hi'
name = "Sam"
```

### `a + b`

Join strings together (this is called concatenation).

```python
print("Py" + "thon")  # Python
```

### `"ab" * 3`

Repeat a string.

```python
print("=" * 10)  # ==========
```

### `f"{x}"`

An f-string: drop variables straight into text inside the curly braces.

```python
age = 12
print(f"I am {age}")  # I am 12
```

### `len(s)`

How many characters are in the string.

```python
print(len("cat"))  # 3
```

### `s[0]`

Get one character by its position. Counting starts at 0.

```python
print("cat"[0])  # c
```

### `s[1:3]`

A slice: the characters from position 1 up to (not including) 3.

```python
print("python"[0:3])  # pyt
```

### `s.upper() / s.lower()`

Make a copy in all capitals, or all lowercase. Handy for comparing answers fairly.

```python
print("Hi".upper())  # HI
if ans.lower() == "yes": ...
```

### `s.title()`

Capitalise the first letter of each word.

```python
print("sam smith".title())  # Sam Smith
```

### `s.strip()`

Remove spaces from the start and end.

```python
print("  hi  ".strip())  # "hi"
```

### `s.replace(a, b)`

Swap every a for b.

```python
print("cat".replace("c", "b"))  # bat
```

### `s.split(sep)`

Break a string into a list of pieces. Splits on spaces if you do not say where.

```python
print("a,b,c".split(","))  # [a, b, c]
```

### `"x" in s`

Is this piece somewhere inside the string? Gives True or False.

```python
print("at" in "cat")  # True
```

### `s.startswith(x) / s.endswith(x)`

Does the string start or end with this?

```python
print("cat.py".endswith(".py"))  # True
```

### `s.isdigit() / s.isalpha()`

Is the string all digits, or all letters?

```python
print("123".isdigit())  # True
```

### `str(x)`

Turn a number (or anything) into a string, so you can join it to text.

```python
print("Score: " + str(10))
```

### `f"{x:.2f}"`

Show a number with an exact number of decimal places. :.2f means 2 decimals, great for money.

```python
price = 3.14159
print(f"${price:.2f}")  # $3.14
```

### `f"{n:>5}"`

Pad a value to a set width so columns line up. > right-aligns, < left-aligns.

```python
print(f"{7:>5}")   # "    7"
```

### `"\n"`

A new line inside a string. \t makes a tab. Use \" to put a quote inside a string.

```python
print("Line 1\nLine 2")
# Line 1
# Line 2
```

## Lists

A list holds many values in order, and you can change it as you go.

### `[1, 2, 3]`

A list. It can hold numbers, strings, anything, in order.

```python
pets = ["cat", "dog", "fish"]
```

### `list[0]`

Get an item by position (starting at 0).

```python
print(pets[0])  # cat
```

### `list[-1]`

Negative counts from the end, so -1 is the last item.

```python
print(pets[-1])  # fish
```

### `len(list)`

How many items are in the list.

```python
print(len(pets))  # 3
```

### `list.append(x)`

Add an item onto the end.

```python
pets.append("bird")
```

### `list.pop()`

Remove and give back the last item (or list.pop(i) for position i).

```python
last = pets.pop()
```

### `list.remove(x)`

Remove the first matching item.

```python
pets.remove("dog")
```

### `x in list`

Is this item in the list? True or False.

```python
print("cat" in pets)  # True
```

### `sorted(list)`

A new list, sorted smallest to largest (or A to Z).

```python
print(sorted([3, 1, 2]))  # [1, 2, 3]
```

### `sum / min / max`

Add up, or find the smallest or largest, of a list of numbers.

```python
print(sum([1, 2, 3]))  # 6
print(max([4, 9, 2]))  # 9
```

### `for x in list`

Do something with each item in turn.

```python
for pet in pets:
    print(pet)
```

## Dictionaries

A dictionary stores pairs: a key, and the value it points to. Like a real dictionary, you look up a word to get its meaning.

### `{"name": "Sam"}`

A dictionary of key: value pairs. Keys are usually strings.

```python
player = {"name": "Sam", "score": 0}
```

### `d[key]`

Look up the value for a key.

```python
print(player["name"])  # Sam
```

### `d[key] = value`

Add a new pair, or change an existing one.

```python
player["score"] = 10
```

### `key in d`

Is this key in the dictionary? True or False.

```python
print("score" in player)  # True
```

### `d.get(key, default)`

Look up a key safely: if it is missing you get the default instead of an error.

```python
player.get("lives", 3)  # 3 if not set
```

### `for k in d`

Loop over the keys. Use d[k] to reach each value.

```python
for k in player:
    print(k, "=", player[k])
```

### `len(d)`

How many pairs are in the dictionary.

```python
print(len(player))  # 2
```

## Tuples

A tuple is like a list, but it cannot be changed after you make it. Handy for pairs that belong together, like an (x, y) point.

### `(1, 2)`

A tuple: values in round brackets, in a fixed order.

```python
point = (100, 200)
```

### `a, b = pair`

Unpack a tuple straight into variables.

```python
x, y = (100, 200)
print(x)  # 100
```

### `point[0]`

Get an item by position, just like a list.

```python
print((100, 200)[1])  # 200
```

## True / False and if

Make your program decide what to do.

### `True / False`

The two boolean values. Comparisons give you one of these.

```python
happy = True
```

### `==  !=`

Equal to, and not equal to. Note the double equals for checking.

```python
print(3 == 3)  # True
print(3 != 5)  # True
```

### `<  >  <=  >=`

Less than, greater than, and the or-equal versions.

```python
print(5 > 3)   # True
print(2 <= 2)  # True
```

### `and  or  not`

Combine conditions. and needs both true, or needs one, not flips it.

```python
if age > 12 and age < 20:
    print("teenager")
```

### `if / elif / else`

Run a block only when a condition is true. elif and else are optional extras.

```python
if score >= 50:
    print("Pass")
else:
    print("Try again")
```

## Loops

Repeat things without copy-pasting.

### `for i in range(n)`

Repeat n times. i counts 0, 1, 2, ... up to n-1.

```python
for i in range(3):
    print(i)   # 0 1 2
```

### `range(a, b)`

Count from a up to (not including) b.

```python
for i in range(1, 4):
    print(i)   # 1 2 3
```

### `range(a, b, step)`

Count in steps. A negative step counts down.

```python
for i in range(5, 0, -1):
    print(i)   # 5 4 3 2 1
```

### `while condition`

Keep repeating as long as the condition stays true. Make sure something changes, or it never stops.

```python
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
```

### `break`

Jump out of a loop straight away.

```python
while True:
    if done: break
```

### `continue`

Skip the rest of this turn and go back to the top of the loop.

```python
for i in range(5):
    if i == 2: continue
    print(i)
```

### `enumerate(list)`

Loop with a counter and the item at the same time.

```python
for i, pet in enumerate(pets):
    print(i, pet)   # 0 cat, 1 dog...
```

### `zip(a, b)`

Loop over two lists together, one pair at a time.

```python
for name, age in zip(names, ages):
    print(name, "is", age)
```

## Functions

Give a chunk of code a name so you can reuse it.

### `def name(args):`

Define your own function. The indented lines run when you call it.

```python
def greet(who):
    print("Hi", who)

greet("Sam")
```

### `return x`

Send a value back out of a function so the caller can use it.

```python
def double(n):
    return n * 2

print(double(5))  # 10
```

## Built-in functions

Handy tools that are always available, no import needed.

### `len(x)`

How many items or characters are in something.

```python
len("cat")  # 3
len([1, 2])  # 2
```

### `range(n)`

A sequence of numbers, mostly used with for loops.

```python
list(range(3))  # [0, 1, 2]
```

### `type(x)`

What kind of thing is x? Useful for working out a bug.

```python
print(type(5))    # int
print(type("a"))  # str
```

### `int / float / str`

Convert between whole numbers, decimals and text.

```python
int("5")    # 5
str(5)      # "5"
```

### `min / max / sum`

Smallest, largest, and total.

```python
max(3, 9, 2)   # 9
```

### `sorted(x)`

A sorted copy of a list or string.

```python
sorted([3, 1, 2])  # [1, 2, 3]
```

## When it goes wrong (errors)

Red errors are not the end of the world, they tell you what to fix. Here are the ones you will meet most.

### `NameError`

You used a name Python does not know: a typo, or a variable you have not made yet.

```python
print(scoer)   # typo of score
# fix: check the spelling
```

### `TypeError`

You mixed types that do not go together, often text and numbers.

```python
print("age " + 5)   # crash
# fix: "age " + str(5)
```

### `ValueError`

The right type but a value that will not work, like turning letters into a number.

```python
int("cat")   # crash
# fix: only int() actual numbers
```

### `IndexError`

You asked for a list or string position that does not exist.

```python
pets = ["cat"]
pets[5]   # crash, there is no [5]
```

### `KeyError`

You asked a dictionary for a key it does not have. Use d.get() to be safe.

```python
player["lives"]   # crash if not set
# fix: player.get("lives", 3)
```

### `IndentationError`

Your spaces are wrong: a line is missing its indent, or they do not line up.

```python
if x > 0:
print("hi")   # needs 4 spaces in front
```

### `SyntaxError`

A typo in the shape of the code: a missing colon, bracket or quote.

```python
if x > 0   # missing the :
    print("hi")
```

## random library

Start with "import random". For dice, shuffles and surprises.

### `random.randint(a, b)`

A random whole number from a to b, including both ends.

```python
import random
random.randint(1, 6)  # a dice roll
```

### `random.random()`

A random decimal from 0.0 up to 1.0.

```python
random.random()  # e.g. 0.37
```

### `random.choice(seq)`

Pick one random item from a list or string.

```python
random.choice(["heads", "tails"])
```

### `random.shuffle(list)`

Shuffle a list into a random order (changes the list itself).

```python
cards = [1, 2, 3]
random.shuffle(cards)
```

### `random.randrange(n)`

A random whole number from 0 up to (not including) n.

```python
random.randrange(10)  # 0..9
```

## math library

Start with "import math". For the trickier sums.

### `math.sqrt(x)`

Square root.

```python
import math
math.sqrt(144)  # 12.0
```

### `math.pi`

The number pi (about 3.14159).

```python
math.pi * r * r   # circle area
```

### `math.floor(x) / math.ceil(x)`

Round down, or round up, to a whole number.

```python
math.floor(3.9)  # 3
math.ceil(3.1)   # 4
```

### `math.pow(a, b)`

a to the power of b (** does this too).

```python
math.pow(2, 10)  # 1024.0
```

### `math.sin / math.cos`

Sine and cosine, in radians. Great for waves and circles.

```python
math.sin(math.pi / 2)  # 1.0
```

### `math.factorial(n)`

n! = n * (n-1) * ... * 1.

```python
math.factorial(5)  # 120
```

## string library

Start with "import string". Ready-made sets of letters, handy for ciphers and puzzles.

### `string.ascii_uppercase`

The capital letters "A" to "Z" as one string.

```python
import string
print(string.ascii_uppercase)  # ABC...Z
```

### `string.ascii_lowercase`

The lowercase letters "a" to "z".

```python
print(string.ascii_lowercase)  # abc...z
```

### `string.digits`

The digits "0" to "9".

```python
print(string.digits)  # 0123456789
```

### `string.ascii_letters`

All the letters, lowercase then uppercase.

```python
print(len(string.ascii_letters))  # 52
```

## statistics library

Start with "import statistics". Averages and spread for a list of numbers.

### `statistics.mean(data)`

The average: add them all up and divide by how many.

```python
import statistics
statistics.mean([2, 4, 6])  # 4
```

### `statistics.median(data)`

The middle value when they are sorted.

```python
statistics.median([1, 5, 2])  # 2
```

### `statistics.mode(data)`

The value that appears most often.

```python
statistics.mode([3, 3, 1])  # 3
```

### `statistics.stdev(data)`

The standard deviation: how spread out the numbers are.

```python
statistics.stdev([2, 4, 6])  # 2.0
```

## time library

Start with "import time". Slow your program down.

### `time.sleep(seconds)`

Pause for a moment. Great for animations and countdowns. (Needs Chrome or Edge in the Playground.)

```python
import time
for i in range(3, 0, -1):
    print(i)
    time.sleep(1)
```

## turtle library

Start with "import turtle" to draw with a little pen. Runs in the Playground.

### `turtle.forward(n)`

Move forward n steps, drawing a line.

```python
import turtle
turtle.forward(100)
```

### `turtle.backward(n)`

Move backwards n steps, still drawing.

```python
turtle.backward(50)
```

### `turtle.left(deg) / turtle.right(deg)`

Turn on the spot by a number of degrees.

```python
turtle.left(90)   # quarter turn
```

### `turtle.goto(x, y)`

Walk straight to a spot. (0, 0) is the centre of the window. turtle.setx and turtle.sety change just one of them.

```python
turtle.penup()
turtle.goto(-100, 50)
turtle.pendown()
```

### `turtle.setheading(deg)`

Face an exact direction: 0 is right, 90 is up, 180 is left, 270 is down. turtle.home() walks back to the centre, facing right.

```python
turtle.setheading(90)   # face up
```

### `turtle.pencolor(c)`

Change the pen colour.

```python
turtle.pencolor("red")
```

### `turtle.pensize(n)`

How thick the line is.

```python
turtle.pensize(5)
```

### `turtle.penup() / turtle.pendown()`

Lift the pen to move without drawing, then put it back down.

```python
turtle.penup()
turtle.forward(50)
turtle.pendown()
```

### `turtle.circle(r)`

Draw a circle of radius r. Add a second number for part of one: circle(40, 180) is a half circle.

```python
turtle.circle(40)
```

### `turtle.begin_fill() / turtle.end_fill()`

Colour a shape in: set turtle.fillcolor, call begin_fill, draw the shape, then end_fill pours the paint.

```python
turtle.fillcolor("gold")
turtle.begin_fill()
turtle.circle(40)
turtle.end_fill()
```

### `turtle.dot(size, color)`

Stamp a filled dot where the turtle stands, no pen needed.

```python
turtle.dot(20, "purple")
```

### `turtle.write(text)`

Write words where the turtle stands. An optional font sets the look: font=("Arial", 20, "normal").

```python
turtle.write("Hi!", font=("Arial", 20, "normal"))
```

### `turtle.bgcolor(c)`

Paint the whole window background.

```python
turtle.bgcolor("#0b1020")
```

### `turtle.speed(n)`

How fast it draws, from 1 (slow) to 10 (fast).

```python
turtle.speed(10)
```

### `turtle.hideturtle() / turtle.showturtle()`

Hide the arrow (the drawing stays), or bring it back. Nice for a clean finished picture.

```python
turtle.hideturtle()
```

### `turtle.xcor() / turtle.ycor() / turtle.heading()`

Where the turtle is and which way it is facing. turtle.position() gives (x, y) together.

```python
if turtle.ycor() > 150:
    turtle.setheading(270)
```

### `turtle.clear() / turtle.reset()`

clear() wipes the drawing but leaves the turtle where it is; reset() wipes everything and sends it home.

```python
turtle.clear()
```

## game library

Start with "import game" to make games: sprites, keys, the mouse and collisions. Full walkthrough and sprite table in the https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/.

### `game.window(w, h)`

Open the game window. Always first. Add background="#0b1020" for a colour.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/window/

```python
import game
game.window(480, 360)
```

### `game.fullscreen()`

Fill the whole screen with the game window, great on phones. Put it right after game.window(). On iPhone it is a full-screen overlay (Safari there has no true fullscreen); on a computer or Android it also asks for real fullscreen. Tap the fullscreen button, the on-screen ✕, or press Esc to leave; game.fullscreen(False) exits from code. A portrait window like 400 x 640 fills a phone best.

```python
game.window(400, 640)
game.fullscreen()
```

### `game.sprite(skin, x, y, size=40, asset=False)`

A sprite you can move around. skin can be a built-in number (0 chicken, 1 dog, 2 bird, 3 egg, 4 coin, 5 basket, 6 shocked, 7 calm, 8 turtle, 9 car, 10 mouse, 11 rocket, 12 asteroid, 13 laser, 14 snake, 15 pacman, 16 ghost, 17 pacman2, 18 kid), its name like "chicken", or any emoji. Add asset=True to use a sprite you designed in the Asset studio, by its id number.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/sprite/

```python
hero = game.sprite("chicken", 100, 200)
mine = game.sprite(5, 300, 200, asset=True)
foe  = game.sprite("🦖", 300, 200)
```

### `game.preload(ids)`

Load your custom Asset-studio art up front (pass an id number, several, or a list) so it is ready the instant you show it instead of popping in the first time. Handy when you set sprite.asset = id while the game is running. Call it once near the top, before the loop.

```python
rots = [7, 8, 9]
game.preload(rots)
# ...later...
plant.asset = random.choice(rots)   # already loaded, no pop-in
```

### `sprite.animate(frames, every=6)`

Flip a sprite through a list of skins on a timer, like a flip-book. Each frame shows for "every" calls to game.frame() (default 6). Pass None to stop. Pac-Man already chomps this way on its own.

```python
star = game.sprite("coin", 200, 120)
star.animate(["🌑", "🌓", "🌕", "🌗"])   # spins
```

### `game.box(x, y, w, h, color, radius)`

A coloured rectangle, centred on (x, y). radius rounds the corners: 0 is square, and anything past half the short side gives a stadium shape. Settable later with box.radius = 10.

```python
btn = game.box(400, 40, 160, 44, "#8a4a12", radius=12)
```

### `game.circle(x, y, w, h, color)`

A coloured circle, centred on (x, y). Leave h out for a round one; give it to squash the circle into an oval, like a hole in the ground.

```python
hole = game.circle(240, 180, 70, 22, "#3d2a1a")
```

### `game.label(text, x, y, size, color, background)`

Draw words (a score or a message), centred on (x, y). color is the text colour; the optional background draws a filled box behind the words so they read on any scene. Labels sit on top of other sprites by default (their .layer starts at 1000).

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/label/

```python
board = game.label("Score: 0", 80, 24, color="#ffffff", background="#000000")
```

### `game.plot(x, y, color, size=2)`

Stamp a dot that STAYS on the screen. Sprites are wiped and redrawn every frame, which is why a few thousand of them crawls; ink is stamped once and then it is just pixels, so a quarter of a million dots still runs at full speed. The right tool for fractals, trails and painting.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/plot/

```python
for i in range(400):
    game.plot(x, y, "#22d3a5")   # builds up a picture
```

### `game.line(x1, y1, x2, y2, color, width=2)`

A stamped stroke, and it stays put like game.plot() does. Use it instead of plot() for anything that moves quickly, or its trail comes out as separate dashes rather than a line.

```python
game.line(old_x, old_y, ship.x, ship.y, "#4ea8ff")
old_x, old_y = ship.x, ship.y
```

### `game.fade(amount=0.05)`

Rub out a fraction of the ink, so trails die away instead of piling up forever. Call it once a frame: 0.02 leaves a long comet tail, 0.2 a short one. The window background shows through as the ink goes.

```python
game.line(old_x, old_y, x, y, "#4ea8ff")
game.fade(0.03)   # the tail behind it decays
game.frame()
```

### `game.wipe()`

Erase all the ink at once and leave the sprites alone. Handy when a setting changes and the drawing so far no longer belongs.

```python
if game.pressed("r"):
    game.wipe()
```

### `game.save_image(surface=None, filename=None, ask=False)`

Save the picture as a PNG on the player's computer. It hands the file to the browser and returns immediately, so it is safe to call inside the game loop. surface=None saves what you can see, sprites and all; surface="ink" saves JUST the stamped layer, so artwork comes out clean with no scoreboard over it. ask=True opens a proper "where shall I put it?" dialog (Chrome and Edge, and only while the keypress is still fresh), otherwise it goes to Downloads.

```python
if game.pressed("s"):
    game.save_image("ink")        # the drawing, with no UI on top
    game.save_image()             # or exactly what is on screen
```

### `game.copy_image(surface=None)`

Put the picture on the clipboard instead of saving it, ready to paste straight into a chat or a post. Same surface choice as game.save_image().

```python
if game.pressed("c"):
    game.copy_image("ink")
```

### `game.pressed(key)`

True while a key is held. "left", "right", "up", "down", "space", or a letter.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/pressed/

```python
if game.pressed("left"):
    bird.x = bird.x - 5
```

### `game.mouse_x() / game.mouse_y()`

Where the mouse pointer is, in game coordinates. game.mouse_in() is True while the pointer is over the game window.

```python
pet.x = game.mouse_x()
pet.y = game.mouse_y()
```

### `game.clicked()`

True once per fresh click on the game window, then False until the next click. One tap, one action: great for buttons and menus.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/clicked/

```python
if plant.at_mouse() and game.clicked():
    plant.size = plant.size + 10
```

### `game.mouse_down()`

True while the mouse button is held, like pressed() but for the mouse.

```python
if game.mouse_down():
    power = power + 1
```

### `game.hide_cursor()`

Hide the real mouse pointer over the game window, so a sprite can be the pointer instead (a watering can, a crosshair). game.show_cursor() brings it back.

```python
game.hide_cursor()
can.x = game.mouse_x()
```

### `sprite.at_mouse()`

True while the mouse pointer is inside this sprite's collision box. Pair with game.clicked() to make clickable sprites and menu buttons.

```python
if start_btn.at_mouse() and game.clicked():
    menu_open = False
```

### `game.textbox(placeholder="", x=None, y=None, width=None)`

A real text box over the game window, for typing that game.pressed() can't do (and the only way to type on a phone). Returns a handle like a sprite: .x, .y, .width place it (default: bottom centre), .placeholder is the grey hint. Read finished lines with .typed(). You can have several.

```python
box = game.textbox("say something...")
while game.playing():
    line = box.typed()
    if line:
        print(line)
    game.frame()
```

### `textbox.typed()`

The line just entered, once, when Enter is pressed (or a Send button submits it), else None. Never blocks, so call it every frame in the loop.

```python
msg = box.typed()
if msg:
    log.append(msg)
```

### `textbox.value / .clear() / .hide() / .show() / .remove()`

value is the current text (read it, or set it to prefill). clear() empties the box; hide(), show() and remove() work like a sprite.

```python
if box.value:
    box.clear()
```

### `game.button(label="", x=None, y=None, width=None, submits=None)`

A clickable button; .clicked() is True once per press. Pass submits=a_textbox and clicking it sends whatever is in that box, the easy way to send on a phone.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/button/

```python
again = game.button("Play again")
if again.clicked():
    reset()
```

### `game.playing()`

The loop condition: true while the game runs.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/frame/

```python
while game.playing():
    game.frame()
```

### `game.frame(fps=30)`

Draw one frame and wait. Put it at the end of the loop. It runs at 30 frames a second by default; try game.frame(60) for extra-smooth motion. Things then move twice as far each second, so halve your step sizes to keep the same speed.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/frame/

```python
game.frame()      # smooth
game.frame(60)    # even smoother
```

### `game.game_over(message, retry=False)`

Show a banner and stop the game. With retry=True a tap or click restarts the game from the top, so players don't have to press Run again (great on phones). Put \n in the message for line breaks.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/game-over/

```python
game.game_over("Game over!\nTap to play again", retry=True)
```

### `game.submit_score(points)`

Records the player's score on the game's per-game leaderboard once you publish it, shown on the game's shared page (best score per player). In the Playground it quietly does nothing, so it is safe to leave in.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/submit-score/

```python
game.submit_score(score)
game.game_over("Score: " + str(score))
```

### `game.sound(n)`

Play a short built-in arcade sound, no files needed: 0 beep, 1 buzz, 2 coin, 3 powerup, 4 jump, 5 laser, 6 hit, 7 explosion, 8 win, 9 lose. The names work too, like game.sound("coin"). Browsers only allow audio after a click, and a game is clicked to play, so it just works.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/sound/

```python
if basket.touches(egg):
    game.sound(2)   # coin
if basket.touches(bomb):
    game.sound(1)   # buzz
```

### `game.save(key, value)`

Remember a value between runs, in this browser, for this program: coins, unlocked levels, a garden's state. value can be a number, text, True/False, or lists/dicts of those. Each program keeps its own save (per browser, not synced across devices). Save when something changes, not every frame.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/save/

```python
game.save("coins", 120)
game.save("plants", ["carrot", "rose"])
```

### `game.load(key, default=None)`

Read back what game.save() stored under key. Returns default the first time, before anything is saved, so a new player starts fresh.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/save/

```python
coins  = game.load("coins", 0)
plants = game.load("plants", [])
```

### `game.clear_save(key=None)`

Forget one saved value, or this whole program's save when you leave the key out (wire it to a "New game" button).

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/save/

```python
game.clear_save("coins")   # just the coins
game.clear_save()          # wipe this game's save
```

### `game.tone(freq, wave="sine", volume=0.15)`

Start a sustained tone and get a handle to steer it live: engines, sirens, drones. Unlike game.sound() (a one-shot), it keeps playing until you .stop() it (or the game ends). Call handle.pitch(hz) and handle.volume(0..1) each frame to change it; wave is "sine", "square", "sawtooth" or "triangle". A low sawtooth whose pitch rises with speed makes a convincing car engine.

```python
engine = game.tone(60, "sawtooth", 0.12)   # idle hum
while game.playing():
    engine.pitch(55 + speed * 12)   # ramps up with acceleration
    engine.volume(0.08 + speed * 0.004)
    game.frame()
engine.stop()
```

### `game.debug(True)`

Draw a red outline around every sprite's hit box: the area touches() checks for collisions. Put it after game.window(). The box turns with .angle and stretches with scale_x and scale_y, exactly like the collisions it shows.

```python
game.window(480, 360)
game.debug(True)
```

### `sprite.x / sprite.y`

Where a sprite is. Change these to move it.

```python
bird.y = bird.y + 5
```

### `sprite.content`

What a sprite shows. Set it to a new skin number, a name, or an emoji to change the picture. A label uses it for its text.

```python
player.content = "coin"
board.content = "Score: " + str(n)
```

### `sprite.angle`

Spin a sprite, in degrees.

```python
coin.angle = coin.angle + 6
```

### `sprite.scale_x / sprite.scale_y`

Stretch or mirror. -1 flips it to face the other way.

```python
chicken.scale_x = -1   # face left (the art faces right)
```

### `sprite.anchor`

The sprite's handle: which point of it sits on (x, y), as fractions of its art, AND the point it spins around. The default (0.5, 0.5) is the middle; (0.5, 1) is the bottom middle, so the sprite stands with its feet on y and swings from its feet like a hammer from its handle; (0, 0) is the top-left corner. The collision box moves and turns with it, so touches() and at_mouse() stay honest.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/anchor/

```python
plant.anchor = (0.5, 1)     # stands on its feet
plant.y = ground_y

hammer.anchor = (0.5, 1)    # swings from the handle
hammer.angle = swing

can.anchor = (0.12, 0.7)    # the spout is the pointer
```

### `sprite.layer`

Which things draw on top. Higher sits above lower; same layer keeps creation order. Everything starts at 0, except labels which start at 1000. Give a sprite a bigger number to draw it over the score.

```python
player.layer = 2000   # over the label
board.layer = 0       # label behind
```

### `a.touches(b)`

True if two sprites overlap. The collision box turns with .angle and stretches with scale, so a rotated sprite checks a rotated box. Use game.debug(True) to see the boxes.

Full page: https://play.pyweblib.org/docs/game/touches/

```python
if basket.touches(egg):
    game.score(1)
```

### `sprite.hitbox`

The collision box size as (width, height). Defaults to roughly fit the art (car wide, egg tall); set your own for a tighter fit, or None for automatic.

```python
car.hitbox = (46, 26)
car.hitbox = None   # back to auto
```

### `sprite.remove()`

Delete a sprite for good (once it is collected or destroyed). Keep many in a list and loop over a copy to remove them safely.

```python
for egg in eggs[:]:
    if car.touches(egg):
        egg.remove()
        eggs.remove(egg)
```

## net library (multiplayer)

Play together. Everyone who joins the same room name sees each other move. Full walkthrough in the multiplayer guide.

### `import net`

Turn on multiplayer. Use it next to import game.

```python
import game, net
```

### `net.join(room)`

Join a room. Anyone who joins the SAME name plays with you. It returns straight away and connects in the background.

```python
net.join("year9-bombers")
```

### `net.join(room, name=, rate=)`

name is what others see you called. rate is how many times a second your position may be sent (1-20). The default 5 looks smooth at 30 fps and costs half what 10 does; raise it only for something twitchy.

```python
net.join("race", name="Sam", rate=8)
```

### `net.me(sprite)`

Show this sprite to everyone else in the room. Call it once per frame, at the end of your loop. Standing still costs nothing: unchanged positions are not resent.

```python
net.me(car)
```

### `net.me(sprite, **extras)`

Send extra facts about yourself along with your position. Others read them back with p.get().

```python
net.me(car, hp=3, ready=True)
```

### `net.others()`

The list of other players. Each one already has a sprite, created, moved and removed for you.

```python
for p in net.others():
    if car.touches(p):
        game.game_over("Crash!")
```

### `player.id`

Who a player is. It does not change while they are playing.

```python
if net.get("bomb") == p.id:
    print(p.name, "has it")
```

### `player.name`

What to call them on screen.

```python
game.label(p.name, p.x, p.y + 30, 12)
```

### `player.x / player.y`

Where that player is.

```python
print(p.name, "is at", p.x, p.y)
```

### `player.sprite`

The sprite drawing that player, if you want to change it yourself.

```python
p.sprite.color = "#ff0044"
```

### `player.get(key, default)`

Read an extra fact they sent with net.me().

```python
if p.get("hp", 0) <= 0:
    print(p.name, "is out!")
```

### `net.set(key, value)`

One fact the whole room shares: who has the bomb, whose turn it is. LAST WRITE WINS, so let only ONE player write each key.

```python
net.set("bomb", net.id)
```

### `net.get(key, default)`

Read a shared value. None until somebody has set it.

```python
if net.get("bomb") == net.id:
    print("Run!")
```

### `net.id`

My own player id. Fixed for this browser tab, so a second tab is a second player.

```python
if net.get("turn") == net.id:
    my_go()
```

### `net.count()`

How many players are in the room, me included.

```python
game.label("Players: " + str(net.count()), 0, 150, 16)
```

### `net.online()`

True once I am really in the room and can be seen. Joining takes a moment.

```python
if not net.online():
    info.content = "Connecting..."
```

### `net.status()`

One of "offline", "joining", "joined", or "unavailable" when this copy of PyWebLib has no multiplayer backend set up.

```python
print(net.status())
```

### `net.room()`

The room name I ended up in. Spaces and punctuation become dashes.

```python
print("You are in", net.room())
```

### `net.leave()`

Leave the room and take everyone else's sprites off my screen.

```python
net.leave()
```

## game3d library

Start with "import game3d" for games in real 3D: shapes in space, a camera you can move, and the same game loop you already know. It is new and deliberately small, so expect shapes and colours rather than models and textures. Coordinates are x right, y up, z towards you, measured in steps rather than pixels, so a box of size 1 is one step wide. Keyboard only for now, so it suits a computer rather than a phone. Try the 3D snippets on the Playground.

### `game3d.background(color)`

The colour behind everything: your sky.

```python
import game3d
game3d.background("#8ec5f0")
```

### `game3d.ground(size=60, y=0, color)`

A big flat floor to stand things on, centred on (0, 0). Nothing stops you walking off the edge, so make it big enough or keep your player inside it yourself.

```python
game3d.ground(40, color="#3f8f4f")
```

### `game3d.box(x, y, z, size=1, color)`

A cube at a point in space. y is how high off the ground it sits, so a size 1 box wants y=0.5 to rest on the floor. Use width, height and depth instead of size to make it a slab or a post.

```python
cube = game3d.box(0, 0.5, 0, color="#e2483d")
wall = game3d.box(0, 1, -5, width=8, height=2, depth=0.4)
```

### `game3d.sphere(x, y, z, size=1, color)`

A ball. size is its width, so it rests on the floor at y = size / 2.

```python
ball = game3d.sphere(3, 0.7, -2, size=1.4, color="#f6c945")
```

### `game3d.cylinder(x, y, z, size=1, color)`

A round post or barrel, standing up. Make it a tall pillar with height, or a thin disc.

```python
post = game3d.cylinder(-2, 1, 0, size=0.6, height=2)
```

### `game3d.camera(x, y, z, look_at=(x, y, z))`

Where you are watching from, and the point you are looking at. Higher y looks down on the scene; bigger z stands further back. fov=80 gives a wider view.

```python
game3d.camera(0, 5, 10, look_at=(0, 0, 0))
```

### `game3d.camera(follow=thing, distance, height)`

Chase a thing instead: the camera sits behind and above it and keeps looking at it, so it follows your player around. Change distance and height to sit closer or higher.

```python
game3d.camera(follow=player, distance=11, height=7)
```

### `game3d.pressed(key)`

True while a key is held, exactly like the 2D game: "left", "right", "up", "down", "space", or a letter.

```python
if game3d.pressed("left"):
    player.x = player.x - 0.25
```

### `game3d.frame(fps=60)`

Draw one frame and wait. Put it at the end of your loop, the same as game.frame().

```python
while True:
    player.spin(ry=2)
    game3d.frame(60)
```

### `thing.x / thing.y / thing.z`

Where a thing is. Change these to move it: x right, y up, z towards the camera (so smaller z is further away).

```python
player.z = player.z - 0.25   # walk away from the camera
```

### `thing.rx / thing.ry / thing.rz`

How far a thing is turned around each axis, in degrees. ry is the usual one: spinning on the spot.

```python
cube.ry = 45
```

### `thing.spin(rx=0, ry=0, rz=0)`

Turn by this much more, every frame, without doing the addition yourself.

```python
coin.spin(ry=3)   # slowly rotates
```

### `thing.move(dx=0, dy=0, dz=0)`

Shift a thing by an amount, instead of setting x, y and z one at a time.

```python
player.move(dx=0.2, dz=-0.1)
```

### `thing.color`

The colour of a thing. Change it whenever you like.

```python
if hurt:
    player.color = "#ffffff"
```

### `thing.visible`

Set it to False to hide a thing without deleting it, and True to bring it back.

```python
ghost.visible = False
```

### `a.touches(b)`

True when two things overlap, checked as boxes around them. Good enough for collecting coins and bumping into walls.

```python
if player.touches(coin):
    coin.remove()
```

### `a.distance_to(b)`

How far apart two things are, in steps. Handy for a proximity check, or for deciding what is closest.

```python
if player.distance_to(enemy) < 3:
    game3d.background("#803030")
```

### `thing.remove()`

Delete a thing for good. Keep them in a list and loop over a copy to remove them safely, exactly like 2D sprites.

```python
for c in coins[:]:
    if player.touches(c):
        c.remove()
        coins.remove(c)
```

### `game3d.tick()`

How many frames have been drawn so far. Useful for timing things without a counter of your own.

```python
if game3d.tick() % 60 == 0:
    print("another second")
```
